title: Mary Cassatt beyond the mother-and-child picture
subtitle: Children, travellers and theatre-goers do not always look where a portrait expects them to.
introduction:
The little girl in the blue armchair has expensive clothes and an entirely informal way of sitting. Cassatt allows those things to coexist. Elsewhere in this selection, a child looks away from an affectionate adult, a woman seals a letter without revealing its contents, and theatre-goers direct their attention beyond the frame.

These pictures give ordinary activity a structure without finishing the story on the figures' behalf. Who looks, who works, and who supports someone else's weight are useful questions to carry through them. The prints sharpen those relationships by reducing shading and giving more work to contour and pattern. Their apparent simplicity rests on carefully chosen positions.
visitNote: The works are held in different collections. Museum names identify holdings, not a promise of display; check the institution before a visit. The colour prints exist in different states and impressions. Each entry links to the particular sheet reproduced, with its accession number where recorded.
selectionNote: Twenty paintings and print designs, each represented by a particular object. The selection is editorial; it is not a complete catalogue or a museum ranking.

books.title: Mary Cassatt, 1844–1926
books.author: Adelyn Dohme Breeskin · National Gallery of Art, 1970
books.note: An exhibition catalogue with an introduction, object entries and reproductions. It provides a broad survey to set beside the narrower thread of everyday activity followed in this guide.

books.title: Mary Cassatt at Work
books.author: Jennifer A. Thompson and Laurel Garber · 2024
books.note: The catalogue considers Cassatt as a professional artist and examines the labour shown in her pictures. Technical research and correspondence add to the questions raised here by The Fitting and the bathing scenes.

works.title: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair
works.catalogueTitle: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair
works.description: The room offers more seating than the child needs, but none of it persuades her into a formal pose. Her sprawling limbs interrupt the upholstered curves around her; the dog has settled into another chair. The contrast with her dressed-up appearance is enough to animate the picture. Whether she is bored, tired or simply comfortable remains open.

works.title: The Loge
works.description: The stage is absent. Instead, Cassatt gives the theatre's spectators the visibility usually reserved for performers. Flowers, bright dress and an open fan make attendance a form of public presentation. The fan partly conceals a face even as its spread attracts attention: an object that belongs to the display can also limit access to the person within it.

works.title: Woman with a Fan
works.description: The fan stretches across the sitter's lap, dividing the portrait into a face above and hands below. A mirror supplies an additional angle on her head and chair. More information does not produce a complete account of the person. Her direct gaze holds its own against the decorative folds and the doubled view behind her.

works.title: The Cup of Tea
works.description: Cup and saucer require the hands to perform different tasks. That small coordination determines the pose within the elaborate hat, gloves and pink dress. The raised cup holds the activity briefly short of drinking. Cassatt finds movement inside a formal social occasion, while the loose colour keeps its carefully observed manners from becoming a rigid diagram.

works.title: Young Girl at a Window
works.description: The window offers depth, but the sitter's immediate attention belongs to the dog on her lap. Contact occupies the foreground while roofs and greenery recede outside. Neither direction cancels the other. The painting can hold a private, absorbed activity and an inhabited world beyond it without making the figure turn outward to explain their relationship.

works.title: Children Playing on the Beach
works.description: Digging involves an awkward grip, bent arms and a body leaning toward its task. Cassatt brings those efforts close, leaving the sea as a narrow distance behind the children. The beach is not chiefly scenery for adults to admire. Buckets and spades give its smallest occupants something demanding to do, and the composition takes that demand seriously.

works.title: Child in a Straw Hat
works.description: With no elaborate setting to supply an anecdote, the joined hands and tilted hat become especially noticeable. The child's unsmiling face need not be translated into a fixed mood. Warm cheeks interrupt the subdued clothes and background; the uneven brim prevents the upright figure from becoming entirely symmetrical. A portrait can be particular without explaining its sitter.

works.title: Girl Arranging Her Hair
works.description: The task generates the pose. One arm reaches back while the other gathers the hair forward, making a set of angles against the close red pattern. Nothing theatrical has to happen for the body to become complicated. The arrangement anticipates a recurring problem in Cassatt's washing and dressing scenes: how to make ordinary coordination clear.

works.title: Mother's Goodnight Kiss
works.medium: Pastel on blue-gray wove paper (faded to tan), mounted on canvas, on a strainer
works.description: The child initiates contact, reaching upward and placing a hand against the adult's cheek. Support from below makes that reach possible. The broad pastel strokes of the garment remain visible around the more closely attended faces. Affection appears as an exchange of movements between bodies of different sizes, rather than as an expression placed on two matching faces.

works.title: Afternoon Tea Party
works.medium: color drypoint, softground etching, and aquatint on laid paper
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: The pale print leaves much of its paper exposed, asking a few curves and light colour areas to establish the meeting. The raised cup is enough to locate a pause in the conversation. This impression should not stand for every version: variations in inking can change the weight of the same design, so the sheet's accession number matters.

works.title: In the Omnibus
works.medium: color drypoint, softground etching, and aquatint on laid paper
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: The bench brings the women close, but their attention goes in different directions. One looks away; the other attends to the baby. The compartment compresses them between a strip of window and the skirts filling the foreground. Public travel and childcare share this small space without merging into a single, harmonious group portrait.

works.title: Maternal Caress
works.medium: color drypoint, softground etching, and aquatint
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: The child wraps an arm around the woman's neck and presses toward her face. A continuous contour gathers the embrace into one shape, while the patterned dress preserves the distinction between their bodies. The adult's lap provides a broad base for an energetic movement above it. Cassatt makes closeness readable through pressure and support.

works.title: The Coiffure
works.medium: color drypoint, softground etching, and aquatint on laid paper
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: A view from behind might conceal the action, but the mirror returns the woman's face and bent shoulders. Her raised arms remain intelligible from both directions. With little shading to round the body, the line of the back becomes decisive. Striped upholstery and patterned wallpaper provide a deliberately busier setting around that restrained contour.

works.title: The Fitting
works.medium: color drypoint, softground etching, and aquatint on laid paper
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: The mirror doubles the standing customer, not the kneeling dressmaker. Display takes up the tall part of the composition; the labour that makes it possible stays close to the floor. The striped gown links the two positions, since its hem is both something to be seen and something requiring adjustment. Fashion appears with its work still attached.

works.title: The Letter
works.medium: color softground etching, drypoint and aquatint on laid paper
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: The writing has finished, but the letter is not yet ready to leave. Cassatt chooses the practical act of sealing the envelope, bringing the paper to the woman's mouth. Its pale surface interrupts the competing patterns of dress and wall. No invented romance is needed: the addressee and contents remain outside the information the image supplies.

works.title: Woman Bathing
works.medium: color drypoint, softground etching, and aquatint on laid paper
works.credit: Mary Cassatt; This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the National Gallery of Art . Please see the Gallery's Open Access Policy .
works.description: The back is almost unshaded, while the skirt's stripes bend around the hips. These are two different ways of describing a body, contour doing one job and pattern another. The mirror adds a second view as the woman leans toward the washstand. Her activity organises the room more decisively than an invitation to look at her does.

works.title: The Boating Party
works.description: The rower's dark back takes a large share of the foreground, preventing the mother and child from becoming the picture's only subject. The curved boat edge encloses all three, with water rising high behind them. Work and leisure face each other across the same confined space. Broad colour areas make that unequal distribution of bodies immediately apparent.

works.title: The Child's Bath
works.description: Washing one foot requires the whole arrangement to cooperate. The adult supports the child on her lap while reaching toward the basin, and both heads incline toward the task. Seen from above, the striped dress and surrounding patterns might scatter attention. The circle of the basin and the linked limbs gather it back around the work of care.

works.title: Breakfast in Bed
works.description: The adult turns toward the child, who looks elsewhere. Physical closeness does not make their attention identical. White pillows and tight framing remove most of the surrounding room, so that small difference in direction carries unusual weight. Cassatt allows the child's separate awareness to remain part of an affectionate scene rather than treating it as a failure of intimacy.

works.title: Woman with a Sunflower
works.description: The child examines a small mirror while a larger one repeats the pair behind them. Looking becomes an activity within the portrait as well as something the viewer does outside it. The sunflower's round centre echoes the handheld glass, but does not need to supply a secret meaning. Shape already connects the objects.

closingSections.title: Leave the figures some privacy
paragraphs: Compare a painting in which two people meet each other's attention with one in which they do not. Cassatt makes room for both. The selection spans several collections and includes prints whose impressions differ; use the object records to identify a particular sheet, and check current display information separately before visiting.
